reader.title: Attempted lynching at Newark (May 1903)
bases: The only report says the people of Newark 'started to lynch a negro' (A1), an attempted or threatened lynching by a crowd.
A1 says the people 'started to lynch' the man, which implies the attempt was not completed, and reports no death; the size of the crowd and any accusation or pretext are not stated.
One editorial paragraph in the Raleigh News & Observer (A1), which itself relays reports in two other papers (the Dispatch and the News) that were not found.

summary.text: The attempted lynching at Newark was an incident on a Sunday in May 1903, probably May 17, in which the people of a town named Newark "started to lynch" an unnamed Black man.

It is known from a single editorial paragraph in the Raleigh News & Observer, which reports no outcome and treated the case chiefly as a quarrel among North Carolina newspapers over where the man came from.
According to the News & Observer of May 20, "The people in Newark started to lynch a negro on Sunday."
The paragraph gives no name for the man, no charge against him, no description of the crowd and no state for Newark.
Its wording implies the attempt was begun but not carried through, and it reports no death or injury.
The Raleigh paper noted that "the Dispatch" called the man "a Wilmington negro" while "the News" claimed he was from Charlotte; neither of those reports appears in the coverage found.

The item opened with the line "North Carolina towns are emulating Atlanta" and closed by saying the paper was glad the man was not from Raleigh, since "this city does not raise negroes who stand a chance of being lynched."
The paragraph ran without a headline among short editorial notes on page 4, and it offered no criticism of the crowd.
No wire report, local Newark account or follow-up appears in the white papers searched, and no Black newspaper in the coverage mentioned the incident.
The man's home was disputed: the Dispatch placed it in Wilmington and the News in Charlotte, both known only through the News & Observer's summary.
The paragraph also leaves open which Newark was meant, and whether its opening reference to North Carolina towns describes Newark or the rival towns claiming the man.

accounts.label: Raleigh News & Observer editorial paragraph
accounts.gist: The people of Newark started to lynch a Black man on Sunday; rival papers disputed whether he came from Wilmington or Charlotte, and the N&O was glad he was not from Raleigh.

accounts.label: The Dispatch (as relayed by the N&O)
accounts.gist: The man was a Wilmington man.

accounts.label: The News (as relayed by the N&O)

framing.detail: No headline; a sardonic civic boast that Raleigh 'does not raise negroes who stand a chance of being lynched' implies the fault lay with the man, with no word against the crowd.

conflicts.note: Both versions are known only through the N&O's relay; neither original report was found.

record_check.dossier: Not stated; the paragraph names only 'Newark'. NC is a guess from the Raleigh paper and the Wilmington/Charlotte dispute, and the man's North Carolina origin being newsworthy suggests the Newark may lie outside the state.
'Started to lynch' reads as an attempt begun and not completed; attempted is at least as well supported as threatened.
'On Sunday' in a 1903-05-20 paper; 1903-05-17 is inferred, not stated.

record_check.record: Papers disagree on whether he was from Wilmington or Charlotte.
record_check.dossier: Correct, but the disagreement is between the Dispatch and the News as relayed by the N&O, the only paper found.

info: A Sunday before 1903-05-20, most likely 1903-05-17 (inferred from 'on Sunday' in a Wednesday paper)
Newark; the paragraph does not name the state
An unnamed Black man ('a negro'), said by the Dispatch to be from Wilmington and by the News to be from Charlotte
